description: I'm a Mechanical Engineering Co-op student at Memorial University with experience in CAD, simulation, Python, and engineering design. I'm passionate about aerospace, spacecraft engineering, and technology. For Space Apps, I'm developing Space Race: Beyond Earth, a strategy game combining realistic spacecraft design, orbital mechanics, and space exploration.
summary:
Space Race: Beyond Earth

Space Race: Beyond Earth is an interactive spacecraft design and space exploration game developed for NASA's Space Mission Design Game challenge. Our project combines strategic gameplay with engineering simulations, allowing players to design spacecraft, plan missions, manage resources, and progressively expand humanity's presence in space.

Through an integrated Engineering Lab and interactive 3D spacecraft builder, players explore how propulsion, power generation, thermal management, payload capacity, mass, and mission economics influence one another. Physics-based calculations evaluate spacecraft feasibility, encouraging players to understand the engineering trade-offs behind their decisions.

The game also incorporates real NASA data, including JPL near-Earth asteroid observations to inform mission opportunities and DONKI space-weather records to influence spacecraft energy-reserve requirements. Orbital planning tools connect these design decisions to mission trajectories.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between complex aerospace engineering and accessible, engaging gameplay, inspiring future engineers while demonstrating the interconnected challenges of real-world space exploration.
details:
Space Race: Beyond Earth

Space Race: Beyond Earth is an interactive, physics-informed space exploration and spacecraft engineering game developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It combines engineering design, orbital mechanics, mission planning, resource management, and economic strategy to make the complexities of space exploration accessible and engaging.

How It Works

Players begin by completing relatively simple Earth-orbit missions and progressively unlock opportunities to explore the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and beyond. Rather than simply selecting a spacecraft and launching it, players must design their own spacecraft, evaluate its engineering feasibility, secure sufficient funding, and manage the mission from launch through operations and evaluation.

Our Engineering Lab connects spacecraft subsystems, including propulsion, electrical power generation, energy storage, thermal management, propellant tanks, communications, and scientific instruments. Changing one component influences others. For example, adding a high-power scientific instrument increases electrical demand, potentially requiring larger solar arrays, additional batteries, and greater thermal radiator capacity. These changes increase spacecraft mass, which affects propulsion requirements, launch costs, and mission feasibility.

An interactive 3D spacecraft builder allows players to visualize their designs and interact with individual components. Players can also save, duplicate, and modify spacecraft configurations for future missions.

The game incorporates an interactive orbital map, spacecraft flight reviews, simulated mission operations, and a research progression system. Players can develop launch capabilities, construct lunar infrastructure, deploy orbital communication and computing networks, and reinvest mission revenue into increasingly ambitious projects.

Integration of NASA and Space Data

A central feature of our project is the integration of publicly available NASA datasets into gameplay.

  • NASA DONKI: Recent solar-flare, geomagnetic-storm, and energetic-particle observations influence simplified spacecraft backup-energy requirements, demonstrating how space weather can affect engineering decisions.
  • NASA JPL Near-Earth Object Web Service: Real asteroid close-approach observations generate time-sensitive fictional observation contracts. Object characteristics influence mission requirements, encouraging players to evaluate their spacecraft's capabilities before accepting opportunities.
  • NASA JPL Horizons: Historical spacecraft trajectory data supports educational visualizations of missions such as Voyager, Dawn, and New Horizons.
  • NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources: Public spacecraft technology references and scientific datasets inform component selections, educational material, and science-focused mission scenarios.

Our orbital tools apply established physics, including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, Keplerian orbital mechanics, and approximate interplanetary transfers. An optional higher-fidelity calculation service supports Lambert transfer analysis and departure-energy comparisons.

Tools and Technologies

The application was developed using TypeScript, React, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, and Vite, with Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei supporting interactive 3D spacecraft visualization. The optional orbital analysis backend uses Java and the Orekit astrodynamics library.

NASA APIs, published engineering references, and public datasets provide scientific context. GitHub supports version control and development, while Vitest and Playwright support automated testing. Browser-based storage preserves campaign progress and spacecraft designs.

Creativity and Intended Impact

Our approach is unique because it combines the accessibility of a strategy game with the interconnected engineering challenges of actual spacecraft design. Instead of presenting spacecraft engineering as isolated equations, players experience how technical decisions affect mission performance, finances, risk, and long-term exploration objectives.

We also incorporated Canadian space-industry inspiration through a progressive domestic launch program, orbital computing infrastructure, satellite communications, and scientific observation missions.

Throughout development, we prioritized engineering interconnectedness, educational accessibility, scientific transparency, and engaging gameplay. Real scientific relationships and published reference data are distinguished from hypothetical game assumptions. The simulations are intended for education and conceptual exploration rather than flight-qualified mission design.

Ultimately, our goal is to inspire students, future engineers, and space enthusiasts by allowing them to experience the challenges of spacecraft design firsthand. By connecting real NASA data with meaningful engineering decisions, Space Race: Beyond Earth transforms complex aerospace concepts into an interactive learning experience where players can discover not just what is possible in space exploration, but why.
